entry.title: Verify before you run
entry.summary: You know the workflow. You describe the task, the AI writes the PowerShell, it looks right, you run it. Most days this works fine. Then September happened. A story went around about an rmdir suggested by AI landing in the wrong place, and a drive disappearing. Generation is a solved problem now. Verification is the part most of us skip. Here is the pass I run before any script written by AI touches a production box. It takes about five minutes. First, read every destructive cmdlet. Search the script for Remove, Stop, Set, Clear, Disable, and Format. For each hit, ask one question: if this runs against the wrong scope, what breaks? AI is confident about syntax and careless about scope. A Remove ADUser with a bad filter is a resume event. Second, run it with WhatIf. It is free information. But know its limits. Not every cmdlet honors WhatIf, and it will not catch logic errors. It catches the obvious disasters, which are the ones that end careers. Third, limit the blast radius before the real run. Run against one test object, one OU, one mailbox. Confirm the output, then widen. If the script has no natural scope limit, that is the review finding. Add one. Two honest caveats. This pass catches accidents, not malice. If you do not trust the source of the script, no checklist saves you. And WhatIf lies by omission. It shows what would happen, not what the script meant to do. Read the logic, not just the preview. The free tool from my last post fits here too. Same idea, other direction. Sanitize logs before they go into the AI, verify scripts before they come out of it. It is free here: https://mightyleo.gumroad.com/l/ojbhki Full disclosure, it is also one of ten tools in a bigger bundle I sell for $19. Thirty environment aware prompts, ten PowerShell tools, ten checklists: https://mightyleo.gumroad.com/l/ai-playbook-for-it-engineers. The sanitizer stays free regardless. If your verify pass catches something good, tell me in the comments. I collect war stories.

entry.title: What a health startup actually has to build before its first feature (and what you can skip)
entry.summary: Every health app starts the same way. You have an idea (a symptom tracker, an AI assistant for lab results, a remote-monitoring dashboard), and before you can ship the first screen that matters, you are designing a database for “a patient’s medical record”. That is where months go. Here is the list we kept running into, and what we decided you should not have to build yourself. The invisible backlog. Before the first real feature, a health product needs: A data model for medical records (measurements, labs, conditions, medications, documents, with units, reference ranges and real measurement dates). None of these is your product. All of them are required before anyone trusts it. Use the standard instead of inventing one. HL7 FHIR R4… the catch is that running a FHIR server well is its own product. That is the part we built as Anpheros: a managed FHIR R4 record per patient, REST API, consent and provenance, hosted in the EU. What the backend looks like on top of it. A code snippet from backend-ts (summary of a record + writing a weight with a LOINC code). Plus two practices worth copying even without Anpheros: it refuses a production key without ALLOW_LIVE=1, and it maps upstream errors to answers the UI can show (401 → 502, 429 → 503, request_id). Try it in about ten minutes. The 30 synthetic patients, curl, npm install @anpheros/sdk / flutter pub add anpheros_sdk, and the other starters (lab, consent, ai-context). What it is not, honestly. Not an EHR. Private beta, single-zone hosting, no contractual SLA, no ISO 27001 / SOC 2 / medical-device certification claimed. Production needs a verified organisation and a signed DPA. It ends with a question to readers: what did they end up building from scratch in their own health project.

entry.title: How TokenCap Traces Taint Flow from Sources to Sinks Using AST Traversal
entry.summary:
Generative AI is great at writing features, but notorious for re-introducing classic security vulnerabilities like SQL injection, Command Injection, and Path Traversal. In TokenCap, we implemented intra-procedural static taint flow analysis in src/security/taint/ to flag tainted data paths before code changes are committed. Sources: HTTP request properties (req.body, req.query, req.params, event.body). Propagation: Data flow tracking across variable assignments, template strings, and object destructuring within the function scope. Sinks: Unescaped database execution calls (db.raw, query()), shell executions (exec, spawn), and filesystem operations (fs.readFile). Sanitizers: Validating functions that cleanse taint (such as parameterized queries or validator schemas). tokencap analyze security
CLI Output: Inspecting 62 route handlers for static taint flow... [WARNING] Potential SQL Injection Sink: - Source: req.query.filter (src/api/users.js:34) - Taint Path: filter -> rawFilterClause -> queryStr - Sink: db.raw(queryStr) (src/api/users.js:48) - Recommendation: Use parameterized binding (:filter) or validate through zod schema.
This security finding is embedded into .tokencap/risk-map.md, alerting any coding agent working on src/api/users.js to avoid raw string concatenation. Read our security architecture at tokencap.vansharora.app
